discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A weather system offshore will move into Oregon and Northern California on Wednesday and weaken. An upper level ridge building offshore on Thursday will move over the area on Friday. Another system stalling offshore will bring a renewed chance of precipitation over the weekend. A more active and impactful weather pattern is expected to develop next week.
hydrology: No river flooding is expected in the next 7 days. However, more widespread precipitation is expected to return early next week for rises on area rivers.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A weather system offshore will move into Oregon and Northern California on Wednesday and weaken. An upper level ridge building offshore on Thursday will move over the area on Friday. Another system stalling offshore will bring a renewed chance of precipitation over the weekend. A more active and impactful weather pattern is expected to develop next week.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Friday)
paragraphs: Mostly quiet weather-wise across western Washington this evening as the region lies between weather systems. A system offshore is slated to take a more southern track on Wednesday moving into Oregon and Northern California. Some of the wrap around moisture from it will spread some light precip northward across the CWA during the day on Wednesday, but locations north of about Everett will probably measure little to nothing in the rain bucket. Conditions will start to dry out again on Thursday with upper ridging offshore moving overhead on Friday. Temperatures through the short term forecast period will be near or slightly below seasonal norms.

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Looking ahead toward the weekend, another upper trough is expected to move into the coastal and/or offshore waters. Ensembles remain at odds with regard to its specific track. Nonetheless, they generally agree that it will come ashore in a weakened state with minimal impacts. Overall QPF looks rather light, but snow levels will be running around 2500 feet so anything that falls at the passes will be in the form of snow.

A trend toward a more active pattern is beginning to take shape toward the early and middle portion of next week. Models are settling into the idea of a 160 to 180 knot jet core entering the central and eastern Pacific and helping carve out a rather deep mean trough position out around 140W. This is expected to send a series of more vigorous frontal systems into the region with more widespread precip, mountain snow, and windy conditions at times. Details will come into better focus in the days ahead.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Cloud coverage will continue to scatter out early this evening with weak high pressure inland, and a front off the coast with VFR at all terminals this evening. The next front will arrive Wednesday morning with showers, arriving roughly from 15- 18Z. High clouds will fill in ahead of the showers from 10-14Z and from south to north. This will likely keep fog potential to a minimal (primarily in low-lying valleys) wide more widespread brief ceiling drops to MVFR likely after 21Z Wednesday afternoon. South to southeast winds this evening will transition to the northeast and northwest tonight into Wednesday with speeds around 5-10 kt. Gusts to 20-25 kt expected along the Olympic/Pacific coastlines.

KSEA...VFR conditions at the terminal through early Wednesday with skies clearing through the afternoon, and then refilling in the morning with showers beginning as early as 20Z. MVFR ceilings are favored briefly from 00Z Thursday through 03-05Z. South/southeast winds will transition to the northeast later this evening into Wednesday around 5-10 kt.
HPR/Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Higher pressure will remain inland today with a low pressure system offshore and associated frontal system moving through tonight into Wednesday. Offshore winds are expected to increase tonight into Wednesday for the coastal waters and western two thirds of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Inherited small craft advisories and gale warnings remain valid and were extended into Wednesday evening as winds and seas decrease. The strongest winds remain most likely to occur in the outer coastal waters. The weather will become more benign across the waters Thursday into Friday with light winds. Additional systems are expected to pass through Saturday into next week, with an increasing potential for storm-force gusts in the coastal waters (currently a 40-50% chance for such occurrence).
Seas: down to 8 to 10 ft Tuesday, increasing back up to 10 to 14 ft on Wednesday, decreasing to 5 to 8 ft Thursday through Saturday before building back up to 10 to 14 ft early next week.
HPR

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: No river flooding is expected in the next 7 days. However, more widespread precipitation is expected to return early next week for rises on area rivers.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active and progressive pattern continues through the next week with chances for rain tonight into Wednesday and from late Friday through this weekend. Dry weather late in the workweek may be accompanied by areas of morning fog.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active and progressive pattern continues through the next week with chances for rain tonight into Wednesday and from late Friday through this weekend. Dry weather late in the workweek may be accompanied by areas of morning fog.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Transient shortwave ridging aloft remains overhead early this afternoon, while an upper low and associated surface frontal system centered well offshore of the Oregon coast will bring widespread chances for precipitation from late this evening into Wednesday. An initial warm front will lift northward, spreading a band of rain to the northeast beginning in Lincoln and Lane Counties by 8-11 PM this evening, and reaching the Columbia River by 1-3 AM Wednesday. A cold front will quickly follow on its heels, yielding another narrow band of rain overnight. Behind that boundary, steady rain will transition to hit-or-miss rain showers which persist through much of Wednesday.

Snow levels of 2500-3500 ft will allow for light accumulations in the Cascades. Chances for 1" of snow from 10 PM this evening through 10 PM Wednesday are 50-80% at the Cascade Passes, higher to the south, but chances for 3" during the same period are only 10-15%. Within the Coast Range, snow is unlikely, only a 10-25% chances for a trace of snow atop the highest peaks. An area of locally lower forecast confidence is within the Hood River Valley, where east winds will bring cooler and drier air which could support light snow or a rain/snow mix. At higher elevations near Dee and Parkdale, a period of light snow appears more likely, with 30-50% chances for accumulating snow of 0.1" or more. At lower elevations from Hood River proper to Odell, the chances for accumulating snow are lower, 10% or less, but short-range ensembles highlight a 20% chance for sufficient diabatic cooling to support at least brief periods of rain/snow mix Wednesday morning. More likely, lower elevation portions of the valley will just see a cold rain.

As the surface low nears the coast, an offshore pressure gradient will also drive east winds across the Cascades, peaking tonight into Wednesday morning. With a maximum pressure gradient of near -4 mb, peak gusts should be expected to reach 30-40 mph in the western Columbia Gorge and far eastern Portland/Vancouver metro, and slightly higher in typical locales favored for gap winds in higher terrain around the Gorge.

Behind this system, there is strong consensus for a period of dry weather from Wednesday night through much of Friday as a narrow upper-level ridge develops along the West Coast. Light winds and lingering surface moisture could allow for the development of radiation fog within sheltered valleys for the Thursday and Friday morning commutes.

Forecast uncertainty increases from late Friday through this weekend as another trough or closed low is favored to approach the coast from the Gulf of Alaska. At this lead time, the majority of long-range ensembles favor the low to be located off the north or central Oregon coast, causing the heaviest rain to occur south of Cape Blanco, while about 35% of members instead depict a scenario with the precipitation maximum occurs farther north in Oregon. In the more likely case where the surface low is located off the north/central Oregon coast, coastal winds may instead be the greatest risk, although there is a less than 10% chance wind gusts exceed 50 mph. -36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Thursday...Mostly clear skies and VFR conditions will give way to increasing high clouds between 00-06Z Wednesday ahead of an incoming frontal system. This system will bring periods of rain to northwest OR and southwest WA, with rain beginning between 06-12Z Wednesday from south to north. Chances for MVFR ceilings increase to 40-70% tonight as rain begins. Conditions will trend towards a mix of MVFR/VFR Wednesday afternoon with rain diminishing.
Gusty easterly winds are expected to develop at KPDX and KTTD sometime between 08-12Z Wednesday, with gusts up to approximately 20 kt at KPDX and 25 kt at KTTD.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions will give way to rain, gusty easterly winds, and lowering ceilings late tonight into Wednesday morning as a frontal system moves in from the south. Chances for ceilings below 3500 ft peak at 65% between 17-19Z Wednesday. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Current observations as of 1 PM Tuesday afternoon show winds slowly building in the outer waters beyond 30 NM as southerly winds are expected to increase with gusts up to 40 kt. Therefore, will maintain the current suite of hazards that include a Gale Warning for zones PZZ271, PZZ272 and PZZ273 along with a Small Craft Advisory for zones PZZ251, PZZ252, PZZ253 and PZZ210.

Winds weaken Wednesday, but with seas remaining elevated around 12-16 ft at 14 seconds due to a fresh westerly swell. Thus the Gale Warning will be replaced with a Hazardous Seas Warning early Wednesday morning through at least Wednesday night. Small Craft Conditions are expected to persist for the inner waters and Columbia River Bar through at least Wednesday night as well.

Calmer conditions arrive on Thursday with seas finally falling below 10 ft and relatively light offshore winds. However, conditions look to ramp up once again for the weekend as yet another system moves towards the coast, bringing southerly winds with gusts up to 40 kt and seas building towards 14-16 ft. /42
